newsitem.title: UK: Nigeria unlikely to meet oil reserves target - study.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria unlikely to meet oil reserves target - study.

text.p: Funding shortfalls and government interference may prevent Nigeria achieving its oil reserves target of 25 billion barrels by 1999, from a current 21 billion, a new report into the Nigerian oil industry says.

"Persistent funding problems of the PJVs (production joint ventures) and continued government interference in NNPC's operations may continue to hamper the realisation of the crude oil reserves target," says the report, Inside Nigerian Oil, published by Petroguide.

Nigeria National Petroleum Corp (NNPC) accounts for 58 percent of Nigerian crude exports through joint venture companies with Western oil companies, but it has consistently failed to find its share of investment on time. At the end of 1994, NNPC was $500 million in arrears, the report says.

The funding issue last month became the focus of tension between government and its partners, when oil minister Dan Etete publicly accused foreign companies of cheating the country of its oil wealth, and demanded they set up escrow accounts in Nigeria so that their investments can be monitored.
"The government and people of Nigeria are not getting their fair share out of the joint venture arrangemnents for petroleum exploration and production," said Etete in August.
He said anomalies and inequalitites which made Nigeria the "laughing stock of the international oil industry" must be eliminated.

But Inside Nigerian Oil says, "Companies operating the joint ventures with NNPC do not receive NNPC cash calls as and when the same fall due, which severely decelerates crude oil production, and results in increased interest charges to the government.".

Because of late payments, the report says NNPC has been asked to concede some of its equity to its joint venture partners, including subsidiaries of Royal Dutch/Shell, Mobil Corp, Chevron Corp, Agip Spa and Elf Aquitaine.

One way of coping with the cash shortages was to sign production sharing contracts with foreign oil companies, which allocate all funding requirements to the foreign partners. Inside Nigerian Oil says this is now the government's favoured method of foreign oil company participation.
